segments.title: Correcting a D-class length error
segments.summary: A follow-up corrects the D-class length figures and shows why even familiar reference books need a second check.
segments.body: Readers' corrections prompted a second look at dimensions used in the earlier D-class discussion. The initial response attributed the discrepancy to figures for particular subclasses because Whitley's cruiser reference had proved reliable before. Checking the book against other sources showed that explanation could not stand. The correction offers a practical historical-method lesson: even a plausible figure needs an independent check of its units and conversion.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke introduces the correction, describes reader feedback, and explains why he returned to the sources.

segments.title: Checking feet-to-metre conversions
segments.summary: The reference book's feet measurements are sound, but several printed metric conversions are not, demonstrating how a trusted source can still introduce error.
segments.body: Whitley's Cruisers of World War II prints correct feet values beside faulty metre conversions for several C-class subclasses. The correction still recommends the book, which had been reliable for other cruiser classes. Those earlier successes made the mistake easier to miss. The disputed dimensions also fitted prior descriptions of the ships' speed and hull form, which helped them escape a second check. Converting the printed feet values independently would have exposed the error before it entered the comparison.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies correct feet figures alongside faulty metre conversions and explains why the error was not caught earlier.

segments.title: Recalculating the cruiser lengths
segments.summary: A live recalculation revises the comparative lengths used in the earlier episode, including one figure that had been overstated by more than ten metres.
segments.body: A fresh conversion gives 143.56 metres for the first three D-class ships, the Danae batch. Rounded to one decimal place, that is 143.6 metres; the book prints 143.5 metres. The C-class comparison gives 137.61 metres against a printed 148.12 metres, a discrepancy described as about 11 metres. The spoken conclusion puts the D class about seven metres longer, although the two quoted lengths differ by about six metres. Both comparisons show the D class as longer and reverse the earlier conclusion. The correction changes the starting point for comparing hull form and expected speed.

evidence.note: The live conversion gives 143.56 metres for the first three D-class ships, rounded verbally to 143.6 against the book's 143.5. The C-class comparison gives 137.61 against 148.12 metres. The spoken seven-metre length advantage differs from the roughly six-metre difference between the quoted lengths.

segments.title: Hull form, power, and the speed question
segments.summary: The revised dimensions leave a half-knot speed puzzle among ships of similar weight and power, with propeller shape identified as a possible variable.
segments.body: A longer, narrower hull generally tends to gain speed for the same horsepower when displacement remains broadly similar. The corrected figures leave the D class slightly longer than the late C-class ships and only somewhat wider in beam. Those proportions suggest about 29.5 knots, yet the cited speed is 29 knots. The half-knot mismatch remains an open design question, with propeller shape proposed as the next variable to investigate.

evidence.note: The transcript connects length, beam, weight, horsepower, and speed before identifying propeller shape as a further question.

segments.title: Why corrections belong in teaching
segments.summary: Reader feedback and a public correction become a practical lesson in checking measurements before using them in historical arguments.
segments.body: The viewers who raised the issue are thanked for doing so carefully and constructively. The mistake is acknowledged, and their intervention shows how criticism can improve historical work. The correction will appear in both teaching material and the cruiser section so students can see that lecturers also need their figures checked. The broader lesson is to trace measurements to their source and verify them before using them in an argument.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke thanks the commenters and says the correction will be used as a teaching example about checking work.
